content: The United States government and private programs are actively working to enhance international collaboration in combating drug abuse and narcotics trafficking. These efforts also aim to promote adherence to international narcotics control treaties, including measures such as eradication of illicit drug production. The Senate Caucus on International Narcotics Control operates as a formal organization within the Senate and holds the status of a standing committee. It possesses subpoena power, allowing it to compel testimony from witnesses and to request the production of books, records, papers, and other documents deemed necessary for its work. Historically, the Caucus has addressed a wide range of issues, including international cooperation, drug eradication, trafficking, interdiction, border control, drug strategy development, evaluations of federal programs, and money laundering concerns. The United States Senate Caucus on International Narcotics Control was initially established as the United States Commission on International Narcotics Control on August 16, 1985, under the Foreign Relations Authorization Act for fiscal years 1986 and 1987. However, its name was changed to the United States Senate Caucus on International Narcotics Control on November 13, 1985, following the Legislative Branch Appropriations Act of 1986. This name change was requested by the House of Representatives to better reflect the group's membership, as no House members were to be appointed to it. The authorizing legislation for the Caucus specifies that its membership is drawn from both the Senate and experts in the private sector. Seven Senators are appointed by the President of the Senate, while five private sector members are appointed by the President of the United States. Of the seven Senators, four are selected from the majority party, including one designated as Chairman, after consultation with the Senate Majority Leader. The remaining three Senators, including one designated as Co-Chairman, are selected from the minority party after consultation with the Senate Minority Leader. The five private sector members of the Caucus are appointed by the President of the United States following consultation with members of the relevant congressional committees. This structure ensures a diverse and expert membership to address the complex challenges of international narcotics control.
